**Subject and central claims.** This section of Steven Pinker's *How the Mind Works* asks when the mind uses crisp theories and when it falls back on fuzzy similarity categories. File page 181 argues that people hold intuitive theories of physics, psychology, logic, arithmetic, biology, kinship and social rules, whose laws can be "played out combinatorially" to predict unseen events. Examples show theory overriding surface similarity: hair colors are grouped by an aging sequence but cloud colors by a rain-making process; a three-inch disk resembles a quarter but is more likely a pizza (quarters are standardized, pizzas vary); a caterpillar and its butterfly are one animal despite looking unlike; a player's jersey color predicts his basket through team coalition (file page 181).

**Why categories are sometimes fuzzy.** Pinker argues that history-driven domains genuinely produce fuzzy categories. Species are fairly lawful (reproductively isolated populations), but higher taxa become "palimpsests" as descendants disperse and adapt differently, so flying is only part of the bird stereotype (file pages 181–182). "Fish" names no single branch of the evolutionary tree: lungfish gave rise to amphibians and so on to reptiles, birds, mammals, so no definition picks out all and only fish (file page 182). Archaeopteryx is "a piss-poor reptile, and not very much of a bird," showing the fuzziness at branch stumps (file page 182).

**Disagreement with Lakoff.** George Lakoff holds that crisp categories are fictions; "mother" and "species" dissolve under scrutiny (surrogate, adoptive, foster mothers; ring species where western mates with central and central with eastern but western cannot mate with eastern) (file page 182). Pinker replies that rule systems are idealizations, never seen pure but still real: triangles without thickness, frictionless planes, ideal gases (file pages 182–183). "Mother" is well defined within mammalian genetics (source of the X-carrying sex cell), evolutionary biology (producer of the larger gamete), physiology (site of prenatal growth), genealogy, and law; the omnibus concept assumes these idealizations coincide (file page 183). Exotic disruptions do not refute the idealized theory, just as friction does not refute Newton (file page 183).

**Stereotypes and ethics.** Pinker notes that some ethnic stereotypes rest on bad statistics, coalitional denigration of outsiders, or fictional media portrayals, but some rest on accurate statistics about real group averages (file page 183). He stresses these statistics say nothing about heredity or cause. A statistically accurate categorizer can still act racist, because racism is wrong not for being irrational but for violating the moral rule against judging individuals by group statistics — a rule system telling us when to switch off statistical categorizers (file pages 183–184).

**Multiple explanatory vocabularies.** The "Core Curriculum" subsection (file page 184) argues that different events demand different explanations: a lawyer's tears are explained by beliefs and desires, her fall by gravitational acceleration of 9.8 meters per second per second. Richard Dawkins's dead bird follows a parabola; a live bird flies away, requiring biological explanation. Artifacts like chairs are explained by intended function. Cognitive scientists posit innate intuitive theories or modules for objects and forces, animate beings, artifacts, minds, natural kinds (file page 184). Pinker warns not to take "theory" or "module" literally: people mix modes, as in "throwing" (intention plus motion), slapstick (person as object), animism, anthropomorphism. He prefers "mental systems, organs, tissues," not encapsulated packages, and adds modes for danger, contamination, status, dominance, fairness, love, friendship, sexuality, children, relatives, self (file page 184).

**Innate capacities versus learned knowledge.** Innate ways of knowing are not innate knowledge: we must learn about Frisbees, butterflies, lawyers. Learning requires couching experience so it generalizes usefully; a VCR records but is not intelligent. Watching lawyers, we record goals and values, not tongue trajectories; goals and values are primitive vocabularies, irreducible to physical concepts (file pages 184–185).

**Limits of a single combinatorial system.** A calculator can multiply but never spell; a word processor can type all combinations but never add. Even digital computers carry distinct hard-wired vocabularies for text, graphics, logic, numbers. Artificial intelligence systems must be endowed with basic categories: objects cannot be in two places at once, animals live for a single interval, people dislike pain (file page 185). A dozen innate vocabularies could still spell all human thought.

**Infant physics.** Against Piaget's sensorimotor infant and William James's "blooming, buzzing confusion," Pinker argues a mechanism must interpret sensation as persisting objects following mechanical laws (file page 185). Elizabeth Spelke and Renee Baillargeon use looking-time: boredom signals the familiar, staring signals surprise (file pages 185–186). Three- to four-month-olds are the youngest tested; results cannot establish innateness, since three-month-olds could have learned, and later abilities could mature without learning (file page 186).

**Object principles.** Spelke and Philip Kelman showed infants treat common motion as the core of objecthood: two sticks moving in tandem behind a screen are expected to be one object even when color and texture differ; static sticks of matching color are not united (file page 186). Other principles: solidity (a panel cannot fall through a cube's space), continuous trajectory (an object cannot teleport between screens), cohesion (parts do not stay behind when lifted), and contact causation (no action at a distance; a ball cannot launch another without touching) (file pages 186, 189).

**Engineering implications (our proposals, not Pinker's).** A thinking machine would need distinct representational vocabularies — physical objects, agency and goals, artifacts and function, biological kinds, social relations — each with its own primitives and inference rules, plus a mechanism for combining them (as "throwing" combines goal and motion). It should support idealized rule systems that tolerate noisy exceptions, and a meta-rule layer that can suspend statistical categorization on ethical grounds. Perception should build object files bound by common motion, with constraints of solidity, continuity, cohesion and contact causation, so ambiguous views can be resolved using stored expectations. Learning must record experience in the right vocabulary (goals, functions, causal powers) rather than raw trajectories, enabling generalization beyond memorized cases. The machine should represent time explicitly (objects persist through intervals), support counterfactual and combinatorial inference over intuitive theories, and keep fuzzy similarity clusters alongside crisp rule-based kinds, choosing between them by domain. Analogy and creativity could arise by mapping structure across these vocabularies; emotions and social cognition would require additional dedicated systems for danger, fairness, status and the like. None of this demonstrates human-level intelligence or consciousness; it is a design sketch grounded in Pinker's claims.

**Uncertainty.** The excerpt contains minor scanning artifacts ("fromdeduction," "Fris-bees," "critics^would") and one garbled passage where the text jumps from file page 186 to later content; page labels shown in braces (for example {310}) are printed page numbers, distinct from file pages.
